title: Symbol Coding
tagline: Year 2 — Symbol substitution, operator substitution, number-word codes and matrix codes

introduction.overview: In symbol coding, letters, words or arithmetic operators are replaced by other symbols according to a key stated in the question. The question gives the key; your job is to apply it exactly. Typical forms are letter-to-symbol codes, substitution of arithmetic operators (when + means ×), number-code to word-code comparisons, and matrix codes where each letter is coded by its row and column.
introduction.placementRelevance: Symbol coding questions are commonly asked in company reasoning rounds. They are rule-following tasks where accuracy matters more than insight.
introduction.realWorldContext: Spreadsheet formulas, cell references such as B7, barcode keys and custom shorthand all rely on exact substitution.

learningObjectives: Apply a letter-to-symbol key to encode and decode words
Evaluate expressions after operator substitution, respecting BODMAS
Deduce word codes from several coded sentences
Encode letters using matrix row and column numbers
Check answers by reversing the substitution

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: BODMAS: Brackets, Orders, Division and Multiplication (left to right), Addition and Subtraction (left to right).

coreDefinitions: Key: the table or statement that tells you what each symbol stands for.
Operator substitution: the symbols +, −, ×, ÷ are given different meanings; first rewrite the expression with the real operators, then evaluate.
Common-element method: in coded sentences, a word common to two sentences matches the code common to them.
Matrix code: a letter is coded by its row and column numbers in a given grid.
Decoding: reversing the key to recover the original.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Symbol coding is a translation exercise. Translate the question into ordinary arithmetic or ordinary letters using the key, solve it, and translate back if needed. Never evaluate the expression with the printed symbols.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: For operator problems, write the real expression directly beneath the printed one, then apply BODMAS to the real expression.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Operator substitution
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Replace each printed symbol by its real operator, then use BODMAS
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Do not evaluate the printed symbols.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Letter-symbol key
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Write the key as a list; encode letter by letter

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Common-element method
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: A word common to two sentences ↔ the code common to them
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Solve one word at a time.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Matrix code
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Code = row number followed by column number

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Check
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Reverse the substitution on your answer

mainNarrative: For letter-symbol keys, build the key as a table and encode each letter in order. With A = @, B = #, C = $, the word CAB becomes $@#, and the code #$@ decodes to BCA.

For operator substitution, rewrite the expression using the real operators. If + means ×, − means ÷, × means + and ÷ means −, then 12 − 4 × 3 + 2 ÷ 1 becomes 12 ÷ 4 + 3 × 2 − 1 = 3 + 6 − 1 = 8. Apply BODMAS after substituting.

For coded sentences, use common elements. If "good morning" = 24, "morning sun" = 45 and "sun rise" = 56, then morning is the common code digit 4, good is 2, sun is 5 and rise is 6. So "good sun" is 25.
For matrix codes, find the letter in the grid; its code is the row number followed by the column number. D is in row 0, column 3, so D = 03; H is in row 1, column 2, so H = 12.
Always verify. Decode your answer with the same key. If it does not return the original, an error crept in.

deepDiveAspects.title: Order of operations after substitution
deepDiveAspects.content: Substitution changes which operators appear, so the order of calculation changes too. Evaluate multiplication and division before addition and subtraction in the real expression.

deepDiveAspects.title: Unique solutions
deepDiveAspects.content: In coded-sentence questions, a unique answer needs each word to appear in at least two sentences. If a word appears only once, its code cannot be fixed by the common-element method.

solvedExamples.title: Operator substitution
solvedExamples.question: If + means ×, − means ÷, × means + and ÷ means −, find the value of 12 − 4 × 3 + 2 ÷ 1.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The real operators decide the order.

solvedExamples.title: Coded sentences
solvedExamples.question: In a code, "good morning" = 24, "morning sun" = 45 and "sun rise" = 56. What is the code for "good sun"?

steps.title: Morning
steps.explanation: Common to the first two: digit 4.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Each word is fixed by a common digit.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Assuming the code follows the word order in a different sentence.

solvedExamples.title: Matrix code
solvedExamples.question: In the letter matrix (rows 0–4, columns 0–4, letters A–Y in order), find the code for HI.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Rows count from the top and columns from the left, starting at 0.

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Work with the printed symbols throughout.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Rewrite using the key, solve in ordinary form, and verify by reversing.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Decode each option and keep the one that returns the original.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Write the key at the side of the page.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Operator-substitution questions are the most common form.
